Stratified PICRUSt2 analysis with inputs and two SDAA directions

stratified-pipeline.Rmd

A change in a community-level function can arise in several ways. A few contributors may increase, many may shift together, or one set of taxa may replace another while the total remains similar. We use stratified PICRUSt2 output to keep the contributor information needed to investigate those patterns.

Our aim is to carry the same biological question through data preparation, statistical testing and plotting. That means deciding on the cohort, comparison and taxonomic rank before fitting, then using those choices consistently when drawing the figures.

Generate stratified PICRUSt2 output

Use representative ASV sequences and the corresponding feature table to obtain the contribution table.

picrust2_pipeline.py \
  -s rep_seqs.fna \
  -i feature-table.tsv \
  -o picrust2_out \
  -p 8 \
  --stratified

Use the appropriate *_contrib.tsv.gz output in the checks below. Replace example file paths and group names with those from your study.

Keep the links intact

The contribution table tells us which ASV contributes to which function in each sample. The phyloseq object supplies the corresponding taxonomy and sample groups. If those identifiers do not match, the analysis cannot reliably connect a contribution to its taxon or cohort.

Keep the ASV identifiers until MicroFun performs the requested aggregation. Aggregating the phyloseq object to genus first can remove the identifiers needed to match the original contribution table and tree tips.

Prepare the stratified inputs

Table 1. Stratified inputs
Input What MicroFun expects
PICRUSt2 contribution table A tab-delimited long table, optionally gzipped, with sample, taxon, function, and taxon_function_abun. Typical filenames include pred_metagenome_contrib.tsv.gz and KO_contrib.tsv.gz.
ASV-level phyloseq object ASV identifiers in its taxonomy rows, a Genus or Class column, and a metadata column for the comparison. Keep ASV identifiers until MicroFun aggregates them.
Optional phylogenetic tree ASV tip labels matching the taxonomy row names. A tree in phyloseq or an explicit Newick file can be used.

The taxon column contains ASV IDs. The function column contains IDs in the selected namespace, such as K00844 for KO. Use raw predicted taxon_function_abun for KO-to-KEGG and direct KEGG runs. Some other modes accept norm_taxon_function_contrib with a compatible backend. Keep contributions finite and nonnegative.

library(phyloseq)

strat_path <- "my_study/KO_contrib.tsv.gz"
ps <- readRDS("my_study/phyloseq_asv.rds")
group_col <- "group"
rank <- "Genus"
reference <- "Control"
target <- "Treatment"

# For an .RData file containing an object named ps, use this load pattern.
# input <- new.env()
# load("my_study/phyloseq_asv.RData", envir = input)
# ps <- input$ps

# If needed, subset the cohort before the checks below.
# ps <- subset_samples(ps, Cohort == "Cohort_A")
# ps <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps) > 0, ps)

stopifnot(file.exists(strat_path), inherits(ps, "phyloseq"))
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
taxonomy <- as(tax_table(ps), "matrix")
stopifnot(group_col %in% names(meta), rank %in% colnames(taxonomy))

selected <- rownames(meta)[meta[[group_col]] %in% c(reference, target)]
ps <- prune_samples(selected, ps)
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
group_counts <- table(factor(meta[[group_col]], levels = c(reference, target)))
print(group_counts)
stopifnot(all(group_counts > 0), sum(group_counts) > 5L)

ids <- data.table::fread(strat_path, select = c("sample", "taxon"),
                         colClasses = "character", showProgress = FALSE)
missing_samples <- setdiff(sample_names(ps), ids$sample)
selected_asvs <- unique(ids$taxon[ids$sample %in% sample_names(ps)])
matched_asvs <- intersect(taxa_names(ps), selected_asvs)
print(c(missing_samples = length(missing_samples),
        matched_asvs = length(matched_asvs),
        contribution_asvs = length(selected_asvs)))
stopifnot(length(missing_samples) == 0L, length(matched_asvs) > 0L)
rm(ids)

Review the overlap before fitting. If IDs use different prefixes or representations, reconcile them from a verified sample or ASV mapping. Extra samples in a contribution file can remain when you analyze a phyloseq subset. Every selected sample must appear somewhere in the file. The default min_samples = 5 requires more than five eligible samples in a table, with at least two groups represented.

Which direction matches your question?

A taxon-centered analysis starts with a microbial contributor and asks about its predicted functional differences. A function-centered analysis starts with a functional feature and asks about its contributors. These views are useful together, but they are not two orientations of one fitted model.

Fit the two SDAA directions

Table 2. The two SDAA directions
Settings with KO input Question Result keys Features within each table
direction = "taxa", pathway = "KO" Within each genus, which predicted KEGG pathways differ by group? Genus KEGG pathway IDs such as ko00010
direction = "function", pathway = "KO" For each KO, which genera contribute differently by group? KO ID Genus

taxon_level = "Class" aggregates ASVs to class in either direction. Set the rank before fitting and use the same rank and sample subset for plots. To analyze a stratified table already containing KEGG pathway IDs, use direction = "taxa", pathway = "KEGG".

For the first KO route, MicroFun sums the contributions of mapped member KOs for each KEGG pathway before fitting, then queries KEGG for annotation. It uses the bundled membership mapping unless you pass kegg_map. When you supply a custom mapping, retain it with the analysis inputs for reproducibility. A KO can belong to multiple pathways, so totals across pathways can include overlapping contributions.

The taxon-centered KO call below needs internet access for KEGG annotation, even though KO-to-pathway membership is read locally. The function-centered KO call retains KOs and does not invoke this pathway annotation step. Academic users do not need a KEGG API key; the requests are handled by KEGGREST. A custom kegg_map changes the local membership table, not the need for annotation access. See local mapping and online annotation.

result_taxa <- pathway_sdaa(
  stratified_path = strat_path, physeq = ps,
  taxon_level = rank, group = group_col,
  direction = "taxa", pathway = "KO",
  daa_method = "Maaslin2", reference = reference,
  p.adjust.method = "BH", threshold = 0.05
)

result_fun <- pathway_sdaa(
  stratified_path = strat_path, physeq = ps,
  taxon_level = rank, group = group_col,
  direction = "function", pathway = "KO",
  daa_method = "Maaslin2", reference = reference,
  p.adjust.method = "BH", threshold = 0.05
)

With Maaslin2, you can pass metadata column names such as confounders = c("Age", "Batch") to account for covariates. MicroFun uses total-sum scaling and an arcsine square-root transformation with this backend. Here group1 is the reference and group2 the target. Positive logFC values are positive model coefficients for the target relative to the reference. In this backend the column stores AST coefficients. Check effect_type when interpreting or reporting the estimates.

The reference group anchors the interpretation of an effect. Decide that direction explicitly instead of inferring it later from the order of group names or the colour of a ribbon. With covariates, the coefficient describes the modeled association conditional on the variables included; it is not a causal effect.

BH is applied within each fitted table. The two KO workflows retain rows with p_adjust < threshold in their result lists. Each direction fits its own models and defines a separate collection of tests.

out <- "MicroFun_results"
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(result_taxa, file.path(out, "sdaa_taxa.rds"))
saveRDS(result_fun, file.path(out, "sdaa_function.rds"))

attr(result_taxa, "microfun")[c("taxon_level", "direction", "function_level")]
head(result_taxa[[1]])
head(result_fun[[1]])

utils::write.table(
  dplyr::bind_rows(result_taxa, .id = "taxon"),
  file.path(out, "sdaa_taxa.tsv"), sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
utils::write.table(
  dplyr::bind_rows(result_fun, .id = "function_id"),
  file.path(out, "sdaa_function.tsv"), sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)

Use the RDS files to resume plotting. They retain the named lists and the microfun attribute, including the analysis rank and direction.

Read the results before plotting

Inspect a few result tables and their recorded settings. Do the keys describe the taxa or functions you expected? Does the saved rank agree with your question? If a result list is empty, review the sample checks, model messages and threshold before trying to force a plot.

Adjustment is applied within each fitted table, not as one global correction across both analysis directions. Keep that scope clear when comparing or reporting findings from multiple taxa and functions.

Reuse the plotting examples

After fitting, run the plot sections with your new result_taxa, result_fun, strat_path and ps. Use names from names(result_taxa) or names(result_fun) when selecting a plot or filtering a Chord. For a phylogeny Sankey, replace the demo tree with a matching tree from your study. For Chord, adapt the example annotation table to your selected IDs or omit function_table to use automatic annotation.

For community-level visualizations, pass a feature-by-sample abundance matrix and matching metadata. Use pathway_daa() to fit sample-level tests for the error-bar plot. To sum an unstratified KO table into KEGG pathways, pass a data frame with KO IDs in its first column to ko2kegg_abundance(data = ...).

See the stratified demonstration for the complete set of example plots.
